item.title: Agentic AI in Automated Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.22522v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated markets increasingly host autonomous, learning trading agents and are powered by formulaic automated market makers (AMMs). We study how heterogeneous agent behavior shapes stress, risk-adjusted performance, liquidity, and volatility in these types of markets. Three behavioral archetypes are modeled as agentic reinforcement learning (RL) systems: a rational arbitrageur, a manipulator, and a retail herd-follower. Each archetype is defined by its reward function within a common, asset-agnostic exposure-control environment, and each is trained with a value-based Deep Q-Network (DQN) and with REINFORCE using a learned baseline. A pilot on hourly cryptocurrency data (AAVE, ETC, SUI) motivates the hypotheses. Herd-followers produce the most frequent but shortest stress episodes, manipulators the fewest but most persistent, and rational agents the most stable rolling Sharpe ratios despite higher return volatility. SHAP attributions tie these patterns to drawdown and cross-asset signals, short-term volatility and position state, and momentum, respectively. The results motivate behavior-specific regulation rather than uniform limits on volatility or turnover.

item.title: Requested, Executed and Recoverable Credit: Shared Action Ordering among LLM Borrowers in a Simulated Lending Market
item.description: arXiv:2610.15973v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We test whether shared action ordering changes executed credit in a simulated collateralized lending market. Three small open-weight language models face a borrowing cap that values collateral at the pool price; only two of the three model families traded. A validation campaign, hash-locked locally before its first model call, pairs 12 common-order markets with 12 balanced-order markets under a revised interface. An exact randomization test rejects the sharp null that common-market net debt is invariant to complete-order assignment (two-sided p = 2/8,100). The pre-specified estimate of the lever-up-first versus delever-first common-market contrast is 1.12 units of initial unused reference borrowing capacity, combining a 0.828 gap between the two groups of common markets with a 0.293 balanced-baseline component. All 24 markets increased debt. An exploratory accounting split shows that lever-up-first common markets borrowed more and repaid less. With requests held fixed, reference-priced collateral narrows the observed common-market order gap from 0.828 to 0.688 capacity units. No market experienced liquidation or realized bad debt. Under the pre-specified fixed-price 30 percent shock benchmark, individual high-LTV loans generate scenario write-offs even though aggregate LTVs remain below the write-off threshold. Most benchmark write-off arises from collateral consumed by the liquidation bonus. The experiment establishes an effect of action order on executed credit; accounting identities and deterministic counterfactuals explain how collateral constraints and borrower-level debt allocation shape conditional creditor recovery.
